question: When claiming hourly rates in a statement of costs for summary assessment in England and Wales, are the guideline hourly rates a cap, and what is needed to justify claiming above them?
reference_answer: The guideline hourly rates are a starting point for summary assessment, not an entitlement or a cap. A rate above the guideline needs a clear and compelling justification (Samsung v LG Display [2022] EWCA Civ 466).
key_points: The guideline hourly rates in effect from 1 January 2026 are a starting point for summary assessment, not an entitlement or a cap | a rate above the guideline needs a clear and compelling justification (Samsung v LG Display [2022] EWCA Civ 466)
authority: Samsung v LG Display [2022] EWCA Civ 466

question: Is a housing disrepair claim by a tenant seeking repairs treated as a small claim in England and Wales?
reference_answer: Only if the repairs are estimated at £1,000 or less and any other damages claimed are £1,000 or less (CPR 26.9(1)(b)). Otherwise it normally goes to the fast track or a higher track, where costs are assessed because fixed recoverable costs do not apply to disrepair claims (CPR 45.1(4)).
key_points: Only if the repairs are estimated at £1,000 or less and any other damages claimed are £1,000 or less (CPR 26.9(1)(b)) | Fixed recoverable costs do not apply to disrepair claims (CPR 45.1(4))

question: In England and Wales, what test applies when a defendant applies to set aside a default judgment that was validly entered, and does the Denton approach come into it?
reference_answer: The court may set the judgment aside if the defendant has a real prospect of successfully defending the claim or there is some other good reason, and must have regard to whether the application was made promptly. The Court of Appeal has held that the Denton tests then apply in full.
key_points: it may set it aside if the defendant has a real prospect of successfully defending the claim, or there is some other good reason (CPR 13.3) | The Court of Appeal has held that the Denton tests then apply in full
authority: CPR 13.3; FXF v English Karate Federation [2023] EWCA Civ 891 at [72]

question: In an English judicial review, can the claimant and defendant simply agree between themselves to extend the time for issuing the claim?
reference_answer: No. The time limits in CPR 54.5 cannot be extended by agreement between the parties. The court can extend time on an application made in the claim form, considering all the circumstances.
key_points: The time limits in CPR 54.5 may not be extended by agreement between the parties (CPR 54.5(2)) | The court can extend time on an application made in the claim form, considering all the circumstances | a defendant's earlier agreement not to take a time point can be relevant to that decision

question: In England and Wales, how far does QOCS protect a personal injury claimant from enforcement of the defendant's costs order, and has that changed recently?
reference_answer: In personal injury claims, costs orders against the claimant are enforceable without permission only up to damages and interest ordered for the claimant or, in claims issued from 6 April 2023, damages, interest and costs ordered or agreed. Strike-out (CPR 44.15) or permission under CPR 44.16 lifts that cap.
key_points: costs orders against the claimant are enforceable without permission only up to damages and interest ordered for it or, in claims issued from 6 April 2023, damages, interest and costs ordered or agreed | Strike-out (CPR 44.15) or permission under CPR 44.16 lifts that cap

question: Can an English court order parties to engage in mediation or other ADR, or is that only possible if they agree?
reference_answer: Yes. In Churchill v Merthyr Tydfil CBC [2023] EWCA Civ 1416 the Court of Appeal held the court can lawfully stay proceedings for, or order, the parties to engage in non-court-based dispute resolution, provided the order does not impair the very essence of the right to a judicial hearing and is proportionate. Since 1 October 2024 the rules say so expressly.
key_points: the court can lawfully stay proceedings for, or order, the parties to engage in a non-court-based dispute resolution process, provided the order does not impair the very essence of the right to a judicial hearing and is proportionate | Since 1 October 2024 the rules say so expressly: the court may order the parties to engage in alternative dispute resolution (CPR 3.1(2)(o))
authority: Churchill v Merthyr Tydfil County Borough Council [2023] EWCA Civ 1416 at [58] and [65]; CPR 3.1(2)(o)

question: How does the basis of assessment, standard or indemnity, change what a bill of costs must withstand on detailed assessment in England and Wales?
reference_answer: On the standard basis proportionality is a live control on recovery. On the indemnity basis it is not, and doubts are resolved in favour of the receiving party.
key_points: On the standard basis proportionality is a live control on recovery | On the indemnity basis it is not, and doubts are resolved in favour of the receiving party

question: In England and Wales, is there a minimum discount a claimant's Part 36 offer must contain for it to count as a genuine attempt to settle?
reference_answer: No. There is no percentage threshold. The court asks whether the offer was a genuine attempt to settle the proceedings, judged on the facts, and the strength of the offeror's case is part of those facts.
key_points: There is no percentage threshold. | The question under CPR 36.17(5)(e) is whether the offer was a genuine attempt to settle the proceedings, judged on the facts. | The strength of the offeror's case is part of those facts.

question: Is there still a limitation period for personal injury claims arising from child sexual abuse in England and Wales?
reference_answer: From 29 June 2026 there is no limitation period for personal injury claims for sexual abuse of someone under 18, including older claims, unless they were settled or decided by a court before then. If brought after the old time limit, the court must dismiss the claim if the defendant shows a fair hearing is not possible. Non-sexual abuse claimed in the same action keeps the 3-year limit and the s.33 discretion.
key_points: Not for personal injury claims for sexual abuse of someone under 18, from 29 June 2026, including older claims, unless settled or decided by a court before then | If the claim is brought after the old time limit, the court must dismiss it if the defendant shows a fair hearing is not possible (s.11ZB) | Physical or other non-sexual abuse claimed in the same action keeps the 3-year limit and the s.33 discretion
authority: Limitation Act 1980 s.11ZA, inserted by s.96 Crime and Policing Act 2026; s.11ZB; KHX v Isle of Wight Council [2026] EWHC 1949 (KB)

question: If a client repudiates a CFA and the solicitor accepts that breach, can the solicitor claim fees on a quantum meruit in England and Wales where the CFA has its own termination provisions?
reference_answer: No. In The Winros Partnership v Global Energy Horizons Corporation [2026] EWCA Civ 654 the Court of Appeal held that no restitutionary remedy was available where the agreement dealt with termination, so the solicitor could not recover beyond what the CFA expressly provided.
key_points: Not where the agreement itself deals with termination. | no restitutionary remedy was available | the solicitor could not recover beyond what the CFA expressly provided
authority: The Winros Partnership v Global Energy Horizons Corporation [2026] EWCA Civ 654

question: In England and Wales, from what date does interest start running on a costs order where the costs are still to be assessed?
reference_answer: Interest runs from the date of the order for costs, even where the costs are still to be assessed (Hunt v R M Douglas (Roofing) Ltd; CPR 40.8). The court can order another date.
key_points: From the date of the order for costs, even where the costs are still to be assessed | The court can order another date
authority: Hunt v R M Douglas (Roofing) Ltd [1990] 1 AC 398; CPR 40.8

question: In England and Wales, if a budgeted phase of my case is running out of money, does that count as a significant development allowing me to vary the costs budget?
reference_answer: No. A phase running out of money is the consequence, not the development. Bassey v Whittaker confirms that without a qualifying significant development there is no power to vary, and the court has no general discretion outside CPR 3.15A.
key_points: A phase running out of money is the consequence, not the development. | Without a qualifying significant development there is no power to vary at all. | The court has no general discretion outside CPR 3.15A.

question: In England and Wales, do the fast track and intermediate track fixed recoverable costs regimes apply to a residential housing disrepair claim?
reference_answer: Generally no. The fast track and intermediate track fixed recoverable costs do not apply to a claim relating to a residential property or dwelling that includes a claim for disrepair, possession or unlawful eviction, unless it arises from a boundary dispute. A claim allocated to the small claims track is limited by CPR 27.14 instead.
key_points: CPR 45.1(4) provides that the fast track and intermediate track fixed recoverable costs do not apply to a claim relating to a residential property or dwelling that includes a claim for disrepair, possession or unlawful eviction | The exception is where the claim arises from a boundary dispute | A claim allocated to the small claims track is limited by CPR 27.14 instead

question: Which precedent form is used for a costs budget in England and Wales, and which is used to apply for a budget variation?
reference_answer: Unless the court orders otherwise, a costs budget uses Precedent H. Precedent R is the budget discussion report and Precedent T is used to seek a variation under CPR 3.15A. The simplified pilot in the Business and Property Courts uses its own forms: Precedent Z, RZ and TZ.
key_points: Unless the court orders otherwise, Precedent H. | Precedent R is the budget discussion report and Precedent T is used to seek a variation under CPR 3.15A. | The simplified pilot in the Business and Property Courts uses its own forms — Precedent Z, RZ and TZ.

question: In England and Wales, when must a statement of costs be filed for a fast track trial where costs are not fixed?
reference_answer: The N260 statement of costs must be filed and served not less than 2 days before a fast track trial. These are clear days, and weekends and bank holidays do not count.
key_points: the N260 statement of costs must be filed and served not less than 2 days before a fast track trial (PD 44 para 9.5(4)(a)) | these are clear days, and weekends and bank holidays do not count (CPR 2.8)

question: In England and Wales, if a claimant with QOCS protection has their claim struck out, can the defendant enforce its costs? Does it make a difference if the claim ends by summary judgment instead?
reference_answer: QOCS protection is lost where the claim is struck out on the CPR 44.15 grounds (no reasonable grounds, abuse of process, or obstructive conduct), and the defendant can then enforce its costs in full without permission. Summary judgment is not a strike-out, so the claimant keeps the protection of CPR 44.14, subject to the CPR 44.16 exceptions such as fundamental dishonesty.
key_points: CPR 44.15 applies only where proceedings are struck out, and summary judgment is not a strike-out | A claimant who loses by summary judgment keeps the protection of CPR 44.14 | Exceptions with permission in CPR 44.16, such as fundamental dishonesty, still apply

question: If a claimant accepts a defendant's Part 36 offer late in a fixed recoverable costs claim in England and Wales, can the defendant get indemnity costs?
reference_answer: No. Late acceptance in a fixed costs claim produces the fixed costs calculation in CPR 36.23. Indemnity costs are a consequence of judgment, not acceptance, and in fixed costs claims CPR 36.24 replaces them with additional costs of 35% of the difference between the fixed costs at expiry and at judgment.
key_points: late acceptance produces the fixed costs calculation in CPR 36.23 | Indemnity costs are a consequence of judgment, not acceptance | CPR 36.24 replaces them with additional costs of 35% of the difference between the fixed costs at expiry and at judgment

question: Is there a time limit for enforcing a judgment or costs order in England and Wales, for example after six years?
reference_answer: Enforcement is not time-barred, but a writ or warrant of control needs the court's permission once six years have passed since the judgment or order. The Limitation Act s.24(1) bars a new action on a judgment after six years, not execution, and no interest more than six years in arrears can be recovered.
key_points: A writ or warrant of control needs the court's permission once six years have passed since the judgment or order (CPR 83.2(3)(a)) | Enforcement itself is not time-barred: s.24(1) of the Limitation Act 1980 stops a new action on a judgment after six years, not execution | no interest more than six years in arrears can be recovered (s.24(2))
authority: CPR 83.2(3)(a); Limitation Act 1980 s.24; Lowsley v Forbes [1999] 1 AC 329

question: How much is the hearing fee on the fast track and on the multi-track, and when must it be paid?
reference_answer: Fee 2.1 is £619 on the fast track and £1,334 on the intermediate track or multi-track. It is paid by the claimant at least 28 days before the trial date (or the Monday of the first week of the trial period) where notice was sent 36 days or more before, and otherwise within 7 days after the notice. If unpaid and no remission applied for, the claim is struck out automatically.
key_points: The hearing fee, fee 2.1, is £619 on the fast track and £1,334 on the intermediate track or multi-track | at least 28 days before the trial date where the court sent out notice of it 36 days or more before, and otherwise within 7 days after the notice | If it is not paid and no remission has been applied for, the claim is struck out automatically
authority: Fees Order Sch 1, notes to fee 2.1; CPR 3.7A1(7)

question: Does a County Court costs order carry interest on judgment debts in England and Wales, or is there a minimum amount?
reference_answer: Only if the judgment or order is for £5,000 or more, or the debt is a qualifying debt under the Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998. A costs order on its own, such as the deemed order on acceptance of a Part 36 offer, needs costs of £5,000 or more.
key_points: Only if the judgment or order is for £5,000 or more, or the debt is a qualifying debt under the Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998 | A costs order on its own needs costs of £5,000 or more

question: Is the 'good reason' test for departing from a budget at detailed assessment the same as the 'significant development' test for revising a budget? In England and Wales civil litigation.
reference_answer: No. They arise at different stages and do different jobs. CPR 3.15A governs revision of the budget during the litigation, while CPR 3.18 governs departure from the approved or agreed figures at detailed assessment.
key_points: They arise at different stages and do different jobs | CPR 3.15A governs revision of the budget during the litigation | CPR 3.18 governs departure from the approved or agreed figures at detailed assessment

question: A housing disrepair claim settled pre-issue for £1,000. Does that automatically mean the claimant's costs are limited to small claims track costs?
reference_answer: No. Smith v Wigan Borough Council [2026] EWHC 660 (SCCO) confirms the settlement figure is not determinative for CPR 46.13 purposes. The court must look holistically at the track the claim would have been allocated to had proceedings been issued.
key_points: the settlement figure is not determinative for CPR 46.13 purposes | the court must look holistically at the track the claim would have been allocated to had proceedings been issued
authority: Smith v Wigan Borough Council [2026] EWHC 660 (SCCO); CPR 46.13

question: Where are the rules for the Stage 3 procedure in the portal claims now found, and what form does the defendant use to acknowledge service in England and Wales?
reference_answer: The Stage 3 Procedure is in Practice Direction 49F, which replaced PD 8B on 1 October 2023. The defendant files and serves an acknowledgment of service in Form N210B not more than 14 days after service of the claim form.
key_points: In Practice Direction 49F, which replaced PD 8B on 1 October 2023 | the defendant files and serves an acknowledgment of service in Form N210B not more than 14 days after service of the claim form (para 8.1) | the court gives at least 21 days' notice of a decision on the papers or a Stage 3 hearing (para 11.2)

question: In England and Wales, if the last day for a step in detailed assessment falls on a weekend or bank holiday, do I get until the next working day both for filing at court and for serving documents on the other side?
reference_answer: Only for acts at the court office, such as filing Form N258, which are in time if done on the next day the court office is open. There is no such extension for serving documents on the other side: a document served on a non-business day is deemed served on a later day, so it must be sent early enough to be deemed served in time.
key_points: For an act at the court office, CPR 2.8(5) makes it in time if done on the next day the court office is open | There is no such extension for serving documents on the other side | A document served on a day that is not a business day is deemed served on a later day (CPR 6.26)

question: Can a litigant in person in England and Wales claim the fixed costs on issue and default judgment in a debt claim?
reference_answer: No. These sums are a legal representative's charges, so a party acting without a solicitor cannot claim them. Unless the court orders otherwise, only the court fees are added.
key_points: These sums are a legal representative's charges (CPR 45.16(1)) | unless the court orders otherwise, only the court fees are added (CPR 45.16(4))

question: When must a bill of costs in a clinical negligence case be served as an electronic bill in England and Wales?
reference_answer: A bill must be electronic where the case is a Part 7 multi-track claim and the bill relates to costs recoverable between the parties for work undertaken after 6 April 2018. Exceptions are fixed or scale costs cases, an unrepresented receiving party, and where the court has otherwise ordered.
key_points: The case is a Part 7 multi-track claim and the bill relates to costs recoverable between the parties for work undertaken after 6 April 2018. | The exceptions are cases subject to fixed costs or scale costs, cases in which the receiving party is unrepresented, and where the court has otherwise ordered.

question: In a fixed recoverable costs housing disrepair claim in England and Wales, what does a claimant get for beating their own Part 36 offer instead of indemnity costs?
reference_answer: Rule 36.24 gives additional costs equivalent to 35% of the difference between the fixed costs for the stage applicable when the relevant period expired and the stage applicable at the date of judgment. It is a formula rather than an assessment.
key_points: additional costs equivalent to 35% of the difference between the fixed costs for the stage applicable when the relevant period expired and the stage applicable at the date of judgment | It is a formula rather than an assessment

question: In England and Wales, does following a pre-action protocol stop the limitation period from running?
reference_answer: No. The Practice Direction and protocols do not alter statutory time limits. If a claim must be issued to stop time running before the protocol is complete, the parties should ask the court for a stay while they comply.
key_points: The Practice Direction and the protocols do not alter the statutory time limits | if a claim has to be issued to stop time running before the protocol is complete, the parties should ask the court for a stay while they comply (PD Pre-Action Conduct para 17)

question: What is the court fee to appeal a small claims track decision in the County Court in England and Wales, and can I recover costs of the appeal?
reference_answer: The court fee is £151 for an appeal in the County Court on the small claims track, from 13 July 2026. The small claims limits on recoverable costs apply to the appeal too, though the cost of an approved transcript reasonably incurred can be recovered.
key_points: The court fee is £151 for an appeal in the County Court on the small claims track (fee 2.3(a)), from 13 July 2026 | The small claims limits on recoverable costs apply to the appeal too, though the cost of an approved transcript reasonably incurred can be recovered (CPR 27.14(2))
authority: Civil Proceedings Fees Order 2008, Sch 1; CPR 27.14(2)

question: In England and Wales, if the court makes an indemnity costs order in a case with an approved costs budget, is the receiving party's recoverable costs capped by that budget?
reference_answer: Not in the ordinary CPR 3.18 sense. CPR 3.18 is directed at standard basis assessment where a costs management order has been made, so on an indemnity assessment the receiving party is not held to the approved budget in the same way, as confirmed in Burgess v Lejonvarn and applied in Lawrence v Associated Newspapers.
key_points: CPR 3.18 is directed at assessment on the standard basis where a costs management order has been made. | On an indemnity assessment the receiving party is not held to the approved budget in the same way.
authority: CPR 3.18; Burgess v Lejonvarn; Lawrence v Associated Newspapers

question: A housing disrepair claim settled before issue and the landlord accepts it must pay costs but disputes the amount. How do I get the costs assessed in England and Wales?
reference_answer: By agreement, or by costs-only proceedings under CPR 46.14. Where everything including liability for costs is agreed but not the amount, either party may issue a Part 8 claim for costs only.
key_points: costs-only proceedings under CPR 46.14 | either party may issue a Part 8 claim for costs only | Paragraph 11 creates the entitlement; CPR 46.14 is the route to quantifying it
authority: CPR 46.14; paragraph 11 of the Pre-Action Protocol for Housing Conditions Claims (England)

question: Can I settle a child's personal injury claim in England and Wales just by agreeing a consent order with the other side?
reference_answer: No. No settlement, compromise or payment relating to a claim by or against a child or protected party is valid without the court's approval. The application for approval includes a draft consent order and the documents in CPR 21.10(3); before proceedings start it is made by a Part 8 claim.
key_points: No settlement, compromise or payment relating to a claim by or against a child or protected party is valid without the court's approval (CPR 21.10(1)). | Before proceedings start, the application is made by a Part 8 claim (CPR 21.10(2)). | Costs payable by or out of the money of a child or protected party normally go to detailed assessment (CPR 46.4(2)).

question: In England and Wales, when is a claim form treated as served if the claimant posts it to a defendant's address within the UK?
reference_answer: A claim form served within the United Kingdom is deemed served on the second business day after completion of the relevant step, such as posting it, leaving it at the address, handing it over or sending the email. A business day excludes Saturdays, Sundays, bank holidays, Good Friday and Christmas Day.
key_points: On the second business day after completion of the relevant step under CPR 7.5(1) | A business day is any day except a Saturday, Sunday, bank holiday, Good Friday or Christmas Day (CPR 6.2(b))

question: A claim issued after October 2023 is re-allocated from the small claims track to the fast track. Which costs regime applies to the claim?
reference_answer: For claims issued on or after 1 October 2023 (with conditions for personal injury claims), a claim moved off the small claims track gets the new track's costs as if allocated there from the outset (CPR 27.15). Costs orders made before allocation are not affected (CPR 46.13(1)).
key_points: For claims issued on or after 1 October 2023 a claim moved off the small claims track gets the new track's costs as if it had been allocated there from the outset | For older claims the small claims rules apply up to re-allocation | Costs orders made before allocation are not affected (CPR 46.13(1))

question: What hourly rate can a litigant in person recover for their own time in a civil costs claim in England and Wales if they can't prove financial loss, and does it apply to work done before October 2025?
reference_answer: The rate is £24 an hour for time reasonably spent on or after 1 October 2025. Time spent before 1 October 2025 stays at the old rate of £19 an hour, whenever the order is made.
key_points: £24 an hour, for time reasonably spent on or after 1 October 2025 | Time spent before 1 October 2025 stays at the old rate of £19 an hour | the new rate applies only to work done on or after that date, whenever the order is made
authority: PD 46 para 3.4, as amended by the 186th Practice Direction Update

question: In detailed assessment proceedings in England and Wales, if the bill is reduced by about 40%, does the receiving party automatically lose the costs of the assessment?
reference_answer: Not automatically. CPR 47.20 requires the court to take the reduction into account, but the court also considers the issues actually won and lost and the overall result of the litigation, as shown in JXX.
key_points: Not automatically. | CPR 47.20 requires the court to take the reduction into account | the court also considers the issues actually won and lost and the overall result of the litigation

question: If a Part 36 offer is made while a claim is in the fixed costs regime and the claim is later allocated to the multi-track before the offer is accepted late, does the fixed costs regime still apply to the costs of acceptance?
reference_answer: Yes. In Attersley v UK Insurance Ltd [2026] EWCA Civ 217 the Court of Appeal held that where the offer was made and the relevant period expired while the claim was in the fixed costs regime, later allocation to the multi-track did not retrospectively displace it, even though acceptance came afterwards.
key_points: where the offer was made and the relevant period expired while the claim was in the fixed costs regime, later allocation to the multi-track did not retrospectively displace it | even though acceptance came afterwards
authority: Attersley v UK Insurance Ltd [2026] EWCA Civ 217

question: How long do I have to bring a personal injury claim in England and Wales, and is the day of the accident counted when working out the last day?
reference_answer: The period is three years from the date the cause of action accrued or, if later, the injured person's date of knowledge. The day of the accident is not counted, so the last day is normally the third anniversary of the accident. The same applies to clinical negligence and industrial disease claims.
key_points: Three years from the date the cause of action accrued or, if later, the injured person's date of knowledge | The day of the accident is not counted, so the last day is normally the third anniversary of the accident
authority: Limitation Act 1980 s.11(4); Marren v Dawson Bentley, approved in Pritam Kaur v S Russell & Sons [1973] QB 336

question: What is the court fee in England and Wales for making an application on notice in a civil case where no other fee is specified?
reference_answer: The current fee is £321 where no other fee is specified.
key_points: The current fee is £321 where no other fee is specified.

question: What is the rate of interest on a sterling judgment debt in England and Wales, and can the court change it?
reference_answer: 8% a year, simple, for judgments given since 1 April 1993. The court can change when interest starts, but not the rate on a judgment in sterling.
key_points: 8% a year, simple | The court can change when interest starts, but not the rate on a judgment in sterling | On a judgment in a foreign currency the court may set the rate
authority: Judgment Debts (Rate of Interest) Order 1993; section 17 of the Judgments Act 1838; County Courts (Interest on Judgment Debts) Order 1991; Horne v Prescot (No 1) Ltd [2019] EWHC 1322 (QB)

question: Is there a standard percentage of the receiving party's costs that the court will usually order as a payment on account of costs in England and Wales?
reference_answer: No. In Cubic Transportation Systems Ltd v Transport for London [2026] EWHC 211 (TCC) the judge accepted there is no fixed percentage of a receiving party's costs which should be awarded. The figure follows the evidence rather than a tariff.
key_points: there is no fixed percentage of a receiving party's costs which should be awarded | The figure follows the evidence rather than a tariff
authority: Cubic Transportation Systems Ltd v Transport for London [2026] EWHC 211 (TCC)

question: When assessing proportionality of costs in a housing disrepair claim in England and Wales, can the value of the repair works be taken into account or only the damages?
reference_answer: Yes. The value of non-monetary relief is expressly included in the proportionality factors, and in housing disrepair it is often the substantial part of what the claim achieved.
key_points: CPR 44.3(5) expressly includes the value of non-monetary relief. | A proportionality argument confined to the damages figure leaves it out.

question: In England and Wales, what is the deadline for taking the step to serve a claim form after it is issued, and does it extend if the last day is a weekend?
reference_answer: The step for the chosen method of service must be taken before midnight on the calendar day four months after the date of issue. Where there is no matching date, the time ends on the last day of the fourth month, and it does not move for a weekend or bank holiday.
key_points: The step for the chosen method must be taken before midnight on the calendar day four months after the date of issue | Where there is no matching date, as for a claim issued on 31 October, the time ends on the last day of the fourth month | It does not move for a weekend or bank holiday

question: In England and Wales, does a claimant who discontinues a claim allocated to the Small Claims Track have to pay the defendant's costs under the usual discontinuance rule?
reference_answer: Not automatically. The general rule that a discontinuing claimant pays the defendant's costs does not apply to Small Claims Track claims, so costs are limited to what CPR 27.14(2) allows, including further costs for unreasonable behaviour under rule 27.14(2)(g).
key_points: CPR 38.6(3) says that rule does not apply to claims allocated to the Small Claims Track. | Costs are limited to what CPR 27.14(2) allows, which includes further costs for unreasonable behaviour under rule 27.14(2)(g).

question: What interim relief can a receiving party get while a detailed assessment is pending in England and Wales, and when can it ask for it?
reference_answer: The court may issue an interim costs certificate for such sum as it considers appropriate under CPR 47.16. It can do so at any time after the receiving party has filed a request for a detailed assessment hearing.
key_points: An interim costs certificate under CPR 47.16 | The court may at any time after the receiving party has filed a request for a detailed assessment hearing issue an interim costs certificate for such sum as it considers appropriate

question: How is the issue fee worked out for a money claim in England and Wales where the sum claimed including interest is over £10,000, and how is it rounded?
reference_answer: Take the sum claimed including interest, multiply by 5% and round down to the nearest penny. For example, a claim of £12,345.79 pays £617.28 because 5% is £617.2895 and the fee is rounded down. The 5% band covers claims over £10,000 and up to £200,000.
key_points: Take the sum claimed including the interest claimed, multiply by 5% and round down to the nearest penny. | The 5% band covers claims over £10,000 and up to £200,000.

question: In a personal injury claim in England and Wales, what rate of interest is awarded on general damages for pain, suffering and loss of amenity, and from when does it run?
reference_answer: Interest on general damages is 2% a year from the date the claim form was served to the date of trial. Bad conduct by the defendant is not a reason to award more.
key_points: 2% a year from the date the claim form was served to the date of trial | Bad conduct by the defendant is not a reason to award more
authority: Jefford v Gee; Birkett v Hayes [1982] 1 WLR 816; Wright v British Railways Board [1983] 2 AC 773; Pawar v JSD Haulage Ltd [2016] EWCA Civ 551 [39]

question: If the Housing Ombudsman has made a maladministration finding against a landlord, does that prove the landlord breached its repairing obligations in a disrepair claim in England and Wales?
reference_answer: No. An Ombudsman finding concerns how the landlord handled the repair and the complaint, not whether it breached section 11 or section 9A of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985. The court makes its own findings on the evidence, so the facts recorded in the determination should be pleaded rather than its conclusion.
key_points: An Ombudsman finding is about how the landlord handled the repair and the complaint, not whether it breached section 11 or section 9A of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985. | The court makes its own findings on the evidence, so plead the facts the determination records rather than its conclusion.
authority: sections 11 and 9A of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985

question: In England and Wales civil proceedings, a client has changed solicitors but no notice of change has been filed yet. Who is treated as the party's solicitor in the meantime?
reference_answer: The former solicitor is treated as the party's solicitor until a notice of change is filed and served, or the court makes an order that the solicitor has ceased to act and that order is served (CPR 42.2(5)).
key_points: The former solicitor is considered to be the party's solicitor unless and until the notice is filed and served | Alternatively, until the court makes an order that the solicitor has ceased to act and the order is served

question: I emailed a claim form to the defendant's solicitors without checking beforehand whether they would accept email service. Is it validly served, and when is it deemed served?
reference_answer: Email is good service only if the person served or their solicitor has said in writing beforehand that they will accept service by email and given the address. A claim form emailed without that was not validly served, as in Barton v Wright Hassall LLP [2018] UKSC 12. If validly emailed, a claim form is deemed served on the second business day after sending.
key_points: Email is good service only if the person served, or their solicitor, has said in writing beforehand that they will accept service by email and given the address | A claim form emailed without that was not validly served in Barton v Wright Hassall LLP [2018] UKSC 12 | A claim form sent by email is deemed served on the second business day after it was sent, whatever the time
authority: PD 6A para 4.1; CPR 6.14; Barton v Wright Hassall LLP [2018] UKSC 12

question: Is mediation compulsory for small claims in England and Wales, for example a defended debt claim issued in the county court in mid-2024?
reference_answer: Under the PD 51ZE pilot, a claim issued on or after 22 May 2024 that would normally be a small claim, where the only remedy claimed is a specified sum of money and it is not a road traffic accident or personal injury claim, is referred to the HMCTS Small Claims Mediation Service once every party has filed its directions questionnaire, without anyone's agreement. The pilot runs to 6 April 2027.
key_points: a claim issued on or after 22 May 2024 that would normally be a small claim, where the only remedy claimed is a specified sum of money and it is not a road traffic accident or personal injury claim, is referred to the HMCTS Small Claims Mediation Service once every party has filed its directions questionnaire, without anyone's agreement | The pilot runs to 6 April 2027

question: Can a defendant in England and Wales get security for costs against a claimant resident in the EU under the current CPR?
reference_answer: Yes, the condition can be met. Since 6 April 2025 it reads that the claimant is resident out of the jurisdiction, with no exception for Hague 2005 or EU states. Whether an order is just depends on a real risk of obstacles to, or extra burden of, enforcement there.

question: What are the Grade A guideline hourly rates for 2026 in England and Wales, and when did they take effect?
reference_answer: The 2026 Grade A Guideline Hourly Rates are £579 for London 1, £422 for London 2, £319 for London 3, £295 for National 1 and £288 for National 2. They took effect on 1 January 2026.
key_points: The 2026 Grade A Guideline Hourly Rates are £579 for London 1, £422 for London 2, £319 for London 3, £295 for National 1 and £288 for National 2. | They took effect on 1 January 2026.

question: I made a Part 36 offer and want to withdraw it before the relevant period ends, but the other side may accept. Does my withdrawal take effect straight away?
reference_answer: Withdrawal must be by written notice served on the offeree, and only if they have not already served acceptance. If served before the relevant period ends, it takes effect only when that period ends, so an acceptance in the meantime stands unless the court gives permission to withdraw.
key_points: A withdrawal, or a change that makes the offer less favourable, served before the relevant period ends takes effect only when it ends. | If the offer is accepted first, the acceptance stands unless the offeror applies for permission within 7 days of the acceptance or, if sooner, before the first day of trial. | The court gives permission only if circumstances have changed and it is in the interests of justice (CPR 36.10).

question: Can a claimant recover interest on future losses in a personal injury claim in England and Wales?
reference_answer: No. A claimant is not kept out of money for a loss still to come, and the same applies to future dependency in a fatal accident claim.
key_points: No. A claimant is not kept out of money for a loss still to come | The same goes for future dependency in a fatal accident claim
authority: Jefford v Gee; Pawar v JSD Haulage Ltd [2016] EWCA Civ 551 [42]; A Train & Sons Ltd v Fletcher [2008] EWCA Civ 413

question: Which costs budget form applies to a costs-managed clinical negligence claim at the County Court at Central London?
reference_answer: Precedent H. The simplified budgeting pilot (Precedent Z) excludes claims to which QOCS applies, and QOCS covers personal injury or death claims, so a clinical negligence claim stays on the standard budgeting rules.
key_points: Precedent H, if the claim is costs managed | The simplified budgeting pilot at the County Court at Central London (PD 51ZG2, Precedent Z) excludes claims to which QOCS applies

question: Do weekends and bank holidays count when calculating CPR time limits in England and Wales, for example a 14 day period?
reference_answer: Only periods of 5 days or less leave out Saturdays, Sundays, bank holidays, Christmas Day and Good Friday. Longer periods count every day, but a filing at court whose period ends on a day the court office is closed is in time on the next day it is open.
key_points: Only periods of 5 days or less leave them out: a Saturday, Sunday, bank holiday, Christmas Day or Good Friday in such a period does not count (CPR 2.8(4)). | Longer periods count every day, but a filing at court whose period ends on a day the court office is closed is in time on the next day it is open (CPR 2.8(5)).

question: Does London weighting apply to fixed costs in England and Wales, and if so which ones and by how much?
reference_answer: Only to the fixed costs in Sections IV, VI, VII and VIII of Part 45, and only where both conditions in CPR 45.3 are met. Those fixed costs, excluding disbursements, then rise by 12.5%.
key_points: Only to the fixed costs in Sections IV, VI, VII and VIII of Part 45 | both conditions in CPR 45.3 are met | Those fixed costs, excluding disbursements, then rise by 12.5%

question: What are the costs caps in an Aarhus Convention judicial review claim in England and Wales, and what must the claimant do to benefit from them?
reference_answer: A claimant cannot be ordered to pay costs above £5,000 if claiming only as an individual, or £10,000 in other cases, and a defendant cannot be ordered to pay above £35,000. The claim form must state it is an Aarhus Convention claim and a verified schedule of financial resources must be filed and served with it.
key_points: a claimant may not be ordered to pay costs above £5,000 where claiming only as an individual, or £10,000 in all other cases, and a defendant not above £35,000 (CPR 46.26) | The limits apply only if the claim form says it is an Aarhus Convention claim and a verified schedule of the claimant's financial resources is filed and served with it (CPR 46.25) | Before 1 October 2023 these rules were CPR 45.41 to 45.45

question: When a court is deciding whether to order indemnity costs in England and Wales, is proportionality of the receiving party's costs a relevant factor?
reference_answer: No. In The New Lottery Company Ltd v The Gambling Commission [2026] EWHC 1311 (TCC), Mrs Justice Joanna Smith held that nothing in the authorities suggests proportionality is relevant to whether to make an indemnity costs order.
key_points: Proportionality is not a relevant factor in considering whether to make an order for indemnity costs | There is nothing in the authorities to suggest proportionality is relevant
authority: The New Lottery Company Ltd v The Gambling Commission [2026] EWHC 1311 (TCC)

question: In England and Wales, how is the additional amount calculated when a claimant beats its own Part 36 offer at trial, and is there a cap?
reference_answer: The court must, unless it is unjust, order an additional amount of 10% of the sum awarded up to £500,000, plus 5% of anything above £500,000, capped at £75,000. The cap is reached at an award of £1 million.
key_points: 10% of the sum awarded up to £500,000, plus 5% of anything above £500,000 | capped at £75,000, so the cap is reached at an award of £1 million | Enhanced interest under CPR 36.17(4)(a) is not payable on the additional amount

question: Does starting charging order proceedings stop interest running on a County Court judgment debt in England and Wales?
reference_answer: No. County Court enforcement that produces a payment stops judgment interest, but charging order proceedings are excluded from that rule.
key_points: charging order proceedings are excluded from that rule | County Court enforcement that produces a payment stops judgment interest
authority: County Courts (Interest on Judgment Debts) Order 1991 art 4(1) and (2)

question: How long does a landlord normally have to respond to a Letter of Claim under the Housing Conditions pre-action protocol in England?
reference_answer: The landlord should normally reply within 20 working days of receipt. Failing to respond in that period is a breach of the protocol and the tenant may then issue proceedings.
key_points: Paragraph 6.2 provides that the landlord should normally reply within 20 working days of receipt | Under paragraph 6.4, failing to respond in that period is a breach of the protocol and the tenant may then issue proceedings
authority: Paragraphs 6.2 and 6.4 of the Pre-Action Protocol for Housing Conditions Claims (England)

question: Can a solicitor sign a statement of truth on behalf of a client in England and Wales, for example on a statement of case or a witness statement?
reference_answer: Yes for a statement of case, an application or a notice of objections, but not for a witness statement, which the maker must sign. The statement refers to the client's belief, and the solicitor's signature is taken as confirming the client authorised it and was told what it means and the consequences of a false statement.
key_points: Yes, in a statement of case, an application or a notice of objections (CPR 22.1(6)(a)(ii)), but not in a witness statement, which the maker signs (CPR 22.1(6)(b)). | The statement refers to the client's belief, not the solicitor's | The signature is taken as the solicitor's statement that the client authorised it and was told what it means and the possible consequences of a false statement (PD 22 para 3.7).

question: Can the parties in English civil proceedings agree between themselves to extend a time limit set by a rule or order that states the consequence of missing it? If so, by how much?
reference_answer: Yes, but only by prior written agreement, by up to a maximum of 28 days, and only if the extension does not put at risk any hearing date, unless the court orders otherwise. Some time limits, such as for an appellant's notice, cannot be extended by agreement at all.
key_points: the parties can extend it only by prior written agreement, by up to a maximum of 28 days, and only if the extension does not put at risk any hearing date, unless the court orders otherwise (CPR 3.8(3) and (4)) | The time for an appellant's notice cannot be extended by agreement at all (CPR 52.15)

question: From what date do the NIHL fixed costs (Table 15) apply to noise induced hearing loss claims in England and Wales?
reference_answer: Annex E applies to NIHL claims where the first letter of claim is sent on or after 1 October 2023.
key_points: Annex E applies to NIHL claims where the first letter of claim is sent on or after 1 October 2023.

question: In England and Wales, what are the response deadlines under the pre-action protocol for disease and noise-induced hearing loss claims? Is the defendant's reasoned answer due within three months?
reference_answer: The defendant must acknowledge within 21 days of the date of posting of the letter of claim, identify all insurers within 30 days of the acknowledgment, and give a reasoned answer within 90 days of the acknowledgment. It is 90 days, not three months. Annex E hearing loss claims likely to suit the fast track, where the first letter of claim was sent on or after 1 October 2023, follow the same timetable.
key_points: An acknowledgment within 21 days of the date of posting of the letter of claim (para 7.1) | all insurers identified within 30 days of the acknowledgment (para 7.2) | a reasoned answer within 90 days of the acknowledgment (para 7.3): 90 days, not three months

question: If the claimants' conditional fee agreements with their solicitor turn out to be unenforceable, can the solicitor's bill of costs still be recovered from the paying party on detailed assessment in England and Wales?
reference_answer: No. In HD & Ors v North Devon Healthcare Trust & Ors [2026] EWHC 2009 (SCCO) the retainers were held unenforceable, so the claimants had no liability to their own solicitor. Under the indemnity principle nothing could be recovered from the defendants, and the assessments were struck out, alternatively assessed at nil.
key_points: The retainers were held unenforceable, so the claimants had no liability to their own solicitor. | The indemnity principle meant nothing could be recovered from the defendants. | The assessments were struck out, alternatively assessed at nil.
authority: HD & Ors v North Devon Healthcare Trust & Ors [2026] EWHC 2009 (SCCO)

question: In England and Wales, does interest keep running on a County Court judgment debt while an attachment of earnings order is in force?
reference_answer: No. No interest accrues while an attachment of earnings order is in force. Taking enforcement proceedings also stops interest on a County Court judgment carrying interest, unless they produce no payment at all.
key_points: No interest accrues while an attachment of earnings order is in force (art 4(3)) | Taking enforcement proceedings stops interest unless they produce no payment at all (County Courts (Interest on Judgment Debts) Order 1991 art 4(1))
authority: County Courts (Interest on Judgment Debts) Order 1991 art 4(1) and art 4(3)

question: Do I need to file the N252 notice of commencement at court to start detailed assessment in England and Wales?
reference_answer: No. Detailed assessment proceedings are commenced by serving the notice and the documents with it (CPR 47.6; PD 47 para 6.2). The court sees the notice later, when the receiving party requests a default costs certificate (N254) or an assessment (N258).
key_points: Detailed assessment proceedings are commenced by serving the notice and the documents with it (CPR 47.6; PD 47 para 6.2) | The court sees the notice later, when the receiving party files a request for a default costs certificate (Form N254) or for an assessment (Form N258)

question: In England and Wales, if I file an application to extend time for a step before the deadline expires but the court only decides it after the deadline has passed, do I have to satisfy the relief from sanctions test?
reference_answer: No. An application to extend time is not an application for relief from sanctions if the application notice is filed before the time expires, even if the court deals with it afterwards. The court decides it under CPR 3.1(2)(a), and applications made in time are looked on more favourably.
key_points: An application to extend the time for a step is not an application for relief from sanctions if the application notice is filed before the time expires, even if the court deals with it afterwards | The court decides it under CPR 3.1(2)(a)

question: Can a claimant recover more than fixed costs in an NIHL claim in England and Wales, for example where the client is vulnerable?
reference_answer: Potentially. CPR 45.9 allows a claim above fixed costs in exceptional circumstances, and CPR 45.10 provides a separate route where vulnerability caused additional work worth at least 20% more than the fixed costs. The tests must actually be met.
key_points: CPR 45.9 allows a claim above fixed costs in exceptional circumstances. | CPR 45.10 provides a separate route where vulnerability caused additional work worth at least 20% more than the fixed costs.

question: In England and Wales civil litigation, if a claimant wins overall but loses an important issue at trial, does that automatically mean they lose the costs associated with that issue?
reference_answer: No. Under CPR 44.2 the court looks at overall success and all the circumstances. Losing an important issue can justify a reduction, as in JBX, but it does not automatically mean all the costs associated with that issue are lost.
key_points: Under CPR 44.2 the court looks at overall success and all the circumstances. | Losing an important issue can justify a reduction | it does not automatically mean that all the costs associated with that issue are lost

question: After the Court of Appeal's decision in Ward v Rai, do Points of Dispute in a detailed assessment still have to comply with the Practice Direction requirements on specificity?
reference_answer: Yes. The Court of Appeal said parties should be under no illusion that paragraph 8.2 of PD 47 requires an Ainsworth compliant approach. Ward decides who chooses the consequence of non-compliance, not whether the requirement exists.
key_points: parties should be under no illusion that paragraph 8.2 of PD 47 requires an Ainsworth compliant approach | Ward decides who chooses the consequence of non-compliance, not whether the requirement exists

question: A defendant accepts a claimant's Part 36 offer to settle the whole claim after the relevant period has expired, and costs liability was not agreed. Who pays what costs under the CPR?
reference_answer: CPR 36.13(5) ordinarily gives the claimant its costs up to expiry of the relevant period and requires the offeree to pay the offeror's costs from expiry to acceptance, unless the court considers that unjust. A late-accepting defendant therefore normally pays the claimant's costs through to acceptance.
key_points: CPR 36.13(5) ordinarily gives the claimant its costs up to expiry of the relevant period and requires the offeree to pay the offeror's costs from expiry to acceptance, unless the court considers that unjust. | Where the defendant is the late-accepting offeree, that normally leaves the defendant paying the claimant's costs through to acceptance.

question: A case has settled and the court previously approved a costs budget. How does the approved budget affect what the receiving party can recover on assessment in England and Wales?
reference_answer: CPR 3.18 means the approved or agreed budget controls recovery for the phases it covers. The bill therefore has to be built to match the last approved budget.
key_points: CPR 3.18 means the approved or agreed budget controls recovery for the phases it covers | the bill has to be built to match it

question: In England and Wales, when must the fast track pre-trial checklist be filed, and what happens if no party files one?
reference_answer: It is due by the date in the notice of allocation, which cannot be more than 8 weeks before the trial date or start of the trial window. If no party files one, the court orders it within 7 days, failing which the claim, defence and any counterclaim are struck out.

question: In England and Wales, how long do I have to appeal a civil court decision, and does time run from the hearing or from when the order is sealed?
reference_answer: The time limit is 21 days after the date of the decision, unless the lower court directs a different period at the hearing where it makes the decision or an adjournment of it. Time runs from the date of the decision hearing, not the date of the sealed order.
key_points: 21 days after the date of the decision, unless the lower court directs a different period | Time runs from the date of the decision hearing, not the date of the sealed order
authority: CPR 52.12(2); McDonald v Rose [2019] EWCA Civ 4 at [21]

question: In England and Wales, can the court award more than the fixed costs on issue, judgment and enforcement in a debt claim, and has a recent case dealt with this?
reference_answer: Yes. The rules apply unless the court orders otherwise, so the court may award more, for example where enforcement is fought hard rather than being simple debt collection (Chedington Events Ltd v Brake [2024] EWHC 384 (Ch)).

authority: CPR 45.16(1); Chedington Events Ltd v Brake [2024] EWHC 384 (Ch), paras 20 to 21

question: If a defendant refuses to pay a claimant's reasonable pre-action costs, can the claimant issue court proceedings solely to recover those costs, or is that an abuse of process in England and Wales?
reference_answer: It is not an abuse of process. In Alphabet (UK) Ltd v AXA Insurance UK Plc [2026] EWHC 674 (SCCO) Costs Judge Brown held that where a defendant refuses to pay costs properly incurred before action, a claimant may issue proceedings to recover them.
key_points: No, it is not an abuse of process to issue proceedings only to recover costs. | Where a defendant refuses to pay costs properly incurred before action, a claimant may issue proceedings to recover them.
authority: Alphabet (UK) Ltd v AXA Insurance UK Plc [2026] EWHC 674 (SCCO)

question: Is it now acceptable to serve a late annotated schedule to support a Point of Dispute shortly before a detailed assessment hearing in England and Wales?
reference_answer: No. The Court of Appeal warned that late variations risk being disallowed or permitted only on conditions, including as to costs. In Ward the paying party succeeded on the point and still faced an adjournment and costs sanctions.
key_points: late variations risk being disallowed or permitted only on conditions, including as to costs | In Ward the paying party succeeded on the point and still faced an adjournment and costs sanctions

question: What is the consequence in England and Wales if a party required to file a costs budget files it late and gets no relief?
reference_answer: The party is treated as having filed a budget comprising only the applicable court fees, unless relief from sanctions is obtained.
key_points: a party required to file a budget which fails to do so will be treated as having filed a budget comprising only the applicable court fees, unless relief is obtained

question: Can a company apply to set aside a statutory demand served on it in England and Wales?
reference_answer: No. The set-aside procedure is for individuals. A demand on a company must tell it that it may apply to the court for an injunction restraining the creditor from presenting or advertising a winding-up petition.

question: In England and Wales, can the parties simply agree to extend the time for filing an appellant's notice if I'm going to miss the deadline?
reference_answer: No. An extension can only be obtained from the appeal court, by including an application for an extension of time in the appellant's notice, stating the reason for the delay and the steps taken before applying. The parties cannot agree to extend the time.

question: If a bill of costs is served without the indemnity-principle certification, does that automatically make service invalid for starting detailed assessment in England and Wales?
reference_answer: No. Duffy v Birmingham City Council [2026] EWCA Civ 146 held that a missing indemnity-principle certification does not automatically invalidate service, and CPR 3.10 can apply to procedural errors. It is not a licence to serve defective bills.

question: If a defendant accepts a claimant's Part 36 offer after the relevant period has expired, is it automatically liable for indemnity costs in England and Wales?
reference_answer: Not automatically. In Fitzpatrick Contractors v Tyco, Coulson J rejected any presumption of indemnity costs from late acceptance alone. Indemnity costs may still be justified by conduct, but that needs its own basis and evidence.

question: In England and Wales, can a judgment debtor be committed for contempt for ignoring an order to attend for questioning if the creditor hasn't paid the debtor's travelling expenses or filed the required affidavit?
reference_answer: No. A judge can hold the person in contempt for failing to comply with the order only if the creditor has complied with CPR 71.4 and 71.5, which cover travelling expenses and the affidavit of service.

question: In England and Wales, how long do I have to put written questions to the other side's expert after their report is served, and does the deadline move if it falls on a weekend?
reference_answer: Part 35 questions must be put within 28 days of service of the expert's report, unless the court gives permission, the other party agrees, or the court's directions give a different date. The 28 days are clear days, so the day of service is not counted, and the date does not move for a weekend or bank holiday.

question: In England and Wales, what limits apply to costs that can be deducted from a child's damages on a settlement approved by the court?
reference_answer: Costs can be deducted only on the litigation friend's application, and only to the extent they were reasonably incurred and are reasonable in amount. At first instance, costs must not exceed 25% of the damages for pain, suffering and loss of amenity and past financial loss.
key_points: Only on the litigation friend's application, and only to the extent the costs or expenses were reasonably incurred and are reasonable in amount (CPR 21.12(1)) | At first instance, costs must not exceed 25% of the damages for pain, suffering and loss of amenity and past financial loss (CPR 21.12(8))

question: Can a defendant get security for costs against an individual claimant living in England and Wales just because the claimant has no money?
reference_answer: No. Poverty alone is not a condition for security against an individual living in England and Wales. Only a company or other body can be caught, where there is reason to believe it will be unable to pay.

question: Can a court in England and Wales assess a bill of costs at nil because of the receiving party's failings in the assessment process?
reference_answer: Yes. CPR 44.11(2)(a) lets the court disallow all or part of the costs being assessed where a party or legal representative has failed to comply with a rule, practice direction or order in connection with the assessment, or where conduct was unreasonable or improper. In Kapoor v Johal the court disallowed everything.
key_points: CPR 44.11(2)(a) lets the court disallow all or part of the costs being assessed | In Kapoor v Johal the court disallowed everything.

question: For guideline hourly rates in England and Wales, does the applicable band depend on the court hearing the case or on where the fee earner works? And which band do Liverpool and Bristol firms fall into?
reference_answer: The band follows the office the fee earner works from, or is mainly attached to, not the court hearing the case. Liverpool and Bristol are National 1.

question: I have a High Court judgment and want an attachment of earnings order against the debtor. Can the High Court make it, and if not what do I do?
reference_answer: No. For a judgment debt only the County Court makes the order. question: In England and Wales, how long do I have to pay costs under a costs order, and from when does the time run if the order was sealed later?
reference_answer: Costs must be paid within 14 days of the date of the judgment or order if it states the amount, or of the costs certificate if the amount is decided by detailed assessment, unless the court specifies another date. The 14 days run from the date the order was made, not when it was sealed or served.
key_points: Within 14 days of the date of the judgment or order if it states the amount, or of the costs certificate if the amount is decided by detailed assessment, unless the court specifies another date. | The 14 days run from the date the order was made, not when it was sealed or served.

question: Do military noise-induced hearing loss claims by former Armed Forces members fall within the NIHL fixed recoverable costs regime in England and Wales?
reference_answer: No. Military claims by members of the Armed Forces in respect of their service career are excluded from the specific NIHL fixed recoverable costs regime in Annex E of the Disease and Illness Pre-Action Protocol.

question: How many days' notice of enforcement must an enforcement agent give a debtor before taking control of goods in England and Wales, and can it be longer?
reference_answer: From 1 May 2026 the notice must be at least 14 clear days (previously 7), or at least 28 where a debt advice provider asks on the debtor's behalf before the notice period ends, unless the debt is non-eligible business debt. Sundays, bank holidays, Good Friday and Christmas Day do not count.

question: After the Mazur litigation in England and Wales, can a costs draftsman still draft a bill of costs, budget, Points of Dispute or Replies for a solicitors' firm?
reference_answer: Yes. Drafting these documents is work carried out for and on behalf of the instructing firm, which retains conduct of the matter, and the Court of Appeal confirmed that delegation on that basis is lawful.

question: When will a court in England and Wales normally carry out a summary assessment of costs rather than order detailed assessment?
reference_answer: The general rule is summary assessment at the conclusion of a fast track trial, and at the conclusion of any other hearing lasting not more than one day, unless there is good reason not to, for example where the paying party substantially disputes the costs.

question: In England and Wales, can I put a second set of questions to an expert on their report, or ask questions that go beyond clarifying the report?
reference_answer: Not without the court's permission or the other party's agreement. Written questions may be put once only, within 28 days of service of the report, and only for the purpose of clarification of the report. They must also be proportionate.

question: In England and Wales, how long before the hearing must an N244 application notice be served on the respondent, and do weekends count?
reference_answer: It must be served as soon as practicable after filing and at least 3 days before the court deals with the application, unless a rule, practice direction or order sets a different time. The 3 days are clear days and, because the period is 5 days or less, weekends and bank holidays do not count.
key_points: at least 3 days before the court is to deal with the application (CPR 23.7(1)) | The 3 days are clear days, so neither the day of service nor the day of the hearing counts | because the period is 5 days or less, weekends and bank holidays do not count either (CPR 2.8)

question: Have fixed recoverable costs been introduced for clinical negligence claims in England and Wales, and who would be responsible for making any rule changes?
reference_answer: No. The Department of Health and Social Care proposed fixed recoverable costs for clinical negligence claims valued between £1,500 and £25,000, with a streamlined pre-action protocol. NHS Resolution's 2025/26 report says the Government has made no announcement on the scheme's future, and the Civil Procedure Rule Committee would be responsible for any rule changes.
key_points: No fixed recoverable costs have been introduced for clinical negligence claims | The proposal covered claims valued between £1,500 and £25,000, with a streamlined pre-action protocol | The Civil Procedure Rule Committee would be responsible for any rule changes

question: Our clinical negligence claim was excluded from costs budgeting because the claimant is a child. Does that mean we can serve a paper bill of costs rather than an electronic one in England and Wales?
reference_answer: No. The exclusions from costs management in CPR 3.12 and the exceptions to the electronic bill requirement in PD 47 paragraph 5.1 are different lists. If it is a Part 7 multi-track claim with post-Transition Date work, paragraph 5.1 applies on its own terms.
key_points: The exclusions from costs management in CPR 3.12 and the exceptions to the electronic bill requirement in PD 47 paragraph 5.1 are different lists. | A claim brought on behalf of a child falls outside the ordinary costs-management regime but is not for that reason outside the electronic bill requirement.
